$comment: Pins the shipped Go and TypeScript HDF validators to one another on JSON Schema `format`. Both read this file and validate the same documents, so the two halves of this repo cannot disagree about whether a document is valid HDF. Each case names the RFC clause that settles it, because a validator disagreeing with its peer is only half the problem — one of them is also wrong.
$resolved: uri and uri-reference were once absent from this table, recorded as a divergence the two libraries could not settle: santhosh-tekuri accepts a space, '<', '|', '^', a backtick, braces and non-ASCII inside a uri-reference where ajv rejects them, and ajv accepts the structurally impossible 'git@github.com:mitre/x.git' and '://example.com' where santhosh-tekuri rejects them. The two lean opposite ways, so matching either would import its errors. Both are now replaced by one RFC 3986 implementation per language, and every row below cites the clause that settles it. Measured over 128 values before the change: the RFC verdict is the stricter of the two libraries everywhere but three rows — it rejects a double quote both accepted, and accepts 'a:' and an IPvFuture host that one side rejected. So no value loses a verdict it held in both languages, and nothing is tightened past the standard.

cases.name: uppercase uuid
cases.why: RFC 4122 §3: generators emit lowercase, but all input is accepted case-insensitively

cases.name: lowercase uuid
cases.why: the canonical spelling

cases.name: uuid with a padded value
cases.why: surrounding whitespace is not part of the UUID grammar

cases.name: not a uuid at all
cases.why: a name is not a UUID

cases.name: lowercase t and z in a date-time
cases.why: RFC 3339 §5.6 NOTE: lowercase t and z are permitted

cases.name: leap second in a date-time
cases.why: RFC 3339 §5.7: second 60 is a leap second and is legal

cases.name: bare date where a date-time belongs
cases.why: RFC 3339 date-time requires full-date T full-time; a bare date is not one

cases.name: date-time with an offset
cases.why: a numeric offset is as valid as Z

cases.name: date-time with no offset at all
cases.why: RFC 3339 requires an offset

cases.name: date-time with an hour-only offset
cases.why: RFC 3339 requires +HH:MM, but ajv-formats accepts a bare hour and so does the Go peer. Pinned as agreement, not as correctness: tightening either side alone would reopen the divergence this table exists to close

cases.name: date-time with a basic-format offset
cases.why: ISO 8601 basic form, which RFC 3339 also excludes and both libraries also accept

cases.name: date-time with a one-digit offset minute
cases.why: the laxness above stops here: neither library accepts a partial minute field

cases.name: space where the T separator belongs
cases.why: RFC 3339 §5.6 permits a space only by mutual agreement; HDF's canonical timestamp requires the T, so every validator in this repo requires it — ajv is tightened to match Go rather than the reverse

cases.name: urn:uuid: prefixed identifier
cases.why: ajv accepts the urn:uuid: form, so the Go peer must too

cases.name: relative path as a system reference
cases.why: RFC 3986 §4.2: a relative-part carrying a path-noscheme is a URI reference

cases.name: rooted path
cases.why: §4.2: path-absolute

cases.name: bare relative segment
cases.why: §4.2: path-noscheme

cases.name: absolute reference with query and fragment
cases.why: §3: scheme, authority, path, query and fragment

cases.name: colon in a later path segment
cases.why: §4.2: only the FIRST segment of a path-noscheme excludes the colon

cases.name: colon shielded by a dot-segment
cases.why: §4.2: the dot-segment is the first segment, so the colon-bearing one is not

cases.name: fragment only
cases.why: §4.4: path-empty plus a fragment is a same-document reference

cases.name: percent-encoded space
cases.why: §2.1: pct-encoded is the correct spelling of a space

cases.name: empty reference
cases.why: §4.2: path-empty is a legal relative-part

cases.name: every sub-delim in a segment
cases.why: §2.2: sub-delims are legal in a path segment

cases.name: tilde in a segment
cases.why: §2.3: the tilde is unreserved

cases.name: ipv6 literal host
cases.why: §3.2.2: an IP-literal carries an IPv6address in brackets

cases.name: ipv4-mapped ipv6 literal host
cases.why: RFC 4291 §2.2 form 3: a trailing dotted quad stands for the last two groups. Each language delegates the address to its own platform parser, so this row is what holds the two to one verdict

cases.name: ipvfuture literal host
cases.why: §3.2.2 IPvFuture. santhosh-tekuri rejects it, so Go is the side that moves here — the RFC, not either library, settles the verdict

cases.name: scp-style remote
cases.why: §4.2: the first segment of a path-noscheme is segment-nz-nc, which excludes the colon, because a reader would otherwise take 'git@github.com' for a scheme. ajv accepts this and is wrong

cases.name: scheme starting with a digit
cases.why: §3.1: a scheme starts with ALPHA, so this can only be read as a relative reference — whose first segment then carries a colon

cases.name: empty scheme
cases.why: §3.1: a scheme is at least one ALPHA

cases.name: a lone colon
cases.why: §4.2: a first segment consisting of one colon is still a first segment containing one

cases.name: raw space
cases.why: §2: SP is outside the character set a URI may contain

cases.name: angle brackets
cases.why: §2: '<' and '>' are excluded; appendix C notes they are the usual delimiters AROUND a URI

cases.name: vertical bar
cases.why: §2: not unreserved, reserved or pct-encoded

cases.name: circumflex
cases.why: §2: not unreserved, reserved or pct-encoded

cases.name: backtick
cases.why: §2: not unreserved, reserved or pct-encoded

cases.name: braces
cases.why: §2: not unreserved, reserved or pct-encoded

cases.name: double quote
cases.why: §2: the double quote is excluded. This is the one value in this table that BOTH libraries accepted — the divergence was never the whole defect

cases.name: backslash
cases.why: §2: the backslash is excluded, which is why a Windows path has to be rewritten rather than carried

cases.name: non-ascii path
cases.why: §2 is ASCII-only: a non-ASCII path is an IRI (RFC 3987), and percent-encoding its UTF-8 is how it becomes a URI reference

cases.name: non-ascii host
cases.why: §3.2.2: an IDN reaches a URI punycoded, not as its Unicode spelling

cases.name: truncated percent escape
cases.why: §2.1: pct-encoded is '%' HEXDIG HEXDIG — two digits, not one

cases.name: non-hex percent escape
cases.why: §2.1: 'zz' are not HEXDIG

cases.name: bare percent
cases.why: §2.1: a literal percent has to be written %25

cases.name: malformed ipv6 literal
cases.why: §3.2.2: three colons are not an IPv6address

cases.name: two elisions in an ipv6 literal
cases.why: RFC 4291 §2.2: '::' may appear once, since two runs of zeros leave the length ambiguous

cases.name: tab inside an ipv6 literal
cases.why: RFC 4291 §2.2: an IPv6address is HEXDIG, ':' and '.' alone. The WHATWG URL host parser removes a tab from anywhere in its input and would read this as '::1', so the character has to be refused before any parser sees it

cases.name: carriage return inside an ipv6 literal
cases.why: RFC 4291 §2.2, and the same removal the WHATWG URL parser applies to CR

cases.name: line feed inside an ipv6 literal
cases.why: RFC 4291 §2.2, and the same removal the WHATWG URL parser applies to LF

cases.name: zone identifier in an ipv6 literal
cases.why: §3.2.2's IP-literal is an IPv6address or an IPvFuture and admits no zone; RFC 6874 adds one, which this dialect does not take. Both platform parsers accept a zone, so it is refused by the character rule

cases.name: percent-encoded zone identifier in an ipv6 literal
cases.why: the RFC 6874 spelling of the row above, refused for the same reason

cases.name: bare dotted quad in brackets
cases.why: §3.2.2: the brackets carry an IPv6address, and an IPv4 host is written without them. Go's netip parses it as a valid address, so an IPv6 one has to be required explicitly

cases.name: leading zeros in an ipv6 literal's dotted quad
cases.why: RFC 4291 §2.2 reads the trailing quad as IPv4address, whose dec-octet (RFC 3986 §3.2.2) has no leading zeros

cases.name: ipv6 literal host in an absolute uri
cases.why: §3.2.2 reached through a scheme, which is the path an implementation takes when it steps past the scheme to find the authority

cases.name: zone identifier in an absolute uri's ipv6 literal
cases.why: the same refusal as the uri-reference row, asserted on the uri production too

cases.name: empty ip literal
cases.why: §3.2.2: the brackets must carry something

cases.name: path separator inside an ipv6 literal
cases.why: §3.2.2: the IP-literal's extent ends at the ']', while §3.2 ends the authority at the first '/', '?' or '#' — so a separator inside the brackets leaves the authority with no closing bracket and no host at all

cases.name: query separator inside an absolute uri's ipv6 literal
cases.why: §3.2.2: the IP-literal's extent ends at the ']', while §3.2 ends the authority at the first '/', '?' or '#' — so a separator inside the brackets leaves the authority with no closing bracket and no host at all, reached here through a scheme

cases.name: brackets around something that is not an address
cases.why: §3.2.2: an IP-literal is an IPv6address or an IPvFuture, nothing else

cases.name: bracketed host with a space before an at-sign
cases.why: RFC 3986 §3.2.2 with §3.2.1: userinfo admits neither '@' nor '[', so an '@' between the brackets belongs to the host and the brackets must still hold an address. Both shipped libraries reject this; an early version of this file's own implementation accepted it by splitting userinfo at the first '@' wherever it fell

cases.name: bracketed host that is two labels round an at-sign
cases.why: RFC 3986 §3.2.2 with §3.2.1: userinfo admits neither '@' nor '[', so an '@' between the brackets belongs to the host and the brackets must still hold an address. Both shipped libraries reject this; an early version of this file's own implementation accepted it by splitting userinfo at the first '@' wherever it fell

cases.name: bracketed host that is only an at-sign
cases.why: RFC 3986 §3.2.2 with §3.2.1: userinfo admits neither '@' nor '[', so an '@' between the brackets belongs to the host and the brackets must still hold an address. Both shipped libraries reject this; an early version of this file's own implementation accepted it by splitting userinfo at the first '@' wherever it fell

cases.why: RFC 3986 §3.2.2 with §3.2.1: userinfo admits neither '@' nor '[', so an '@' between the brackets belongs to the host and the brackets must still hold an address. Both shipped libraries reject this; an early version of this file's own implementation accepted it by splitting userinfo at the first '@' wherever it fell

cases.name: bracketed address followed by an at-sign
cases.why: RFC 3986 §3.2.2 with §3.2.1: userinfo admits neither '@' nor '[', so an '@' between the brackets belongs to the host and the brackets must still hold an address. Both shipped libraries reject this; an early version of this file's own implementation accepted it by splitting userinfo at the first '@' wherever it fell

cases.name: bracketed host with non-ascii before an at-sign
cases.why: RFC 3986 §3.2.2 with §3.2.1: userinfo admits neither '@' nor '[', so an '@' between the brackets belongs to the host and the brackets must still hold an address. Both shipped libraries reject this; an early version of this file's own implementation accepted it by splitting userinfo at the first '@' wherever it fell

cases.name: bracketed host with excluded characters before an at-sign
cases.why: RFC 3986 §3.2.2 with §3.2.1: userinfo admits neither '@' nor '[', so an '@' between the brackets belongs to the host and the brackets must still hold an address. Both shipped libraries reject this; an early version of this file's own implementation accepted it by splitting userinfo at the first '@' wherever it fell

cases.name: bracketed host with a double quote before an at-sign
cases.why: RFC 3986 §3.2.2 with §3.2.1: userinfo admits neither '@' nor '[', so an '@' between the brackets belongs to the host and the brackets must still hold an address. Both shipped libraries reject this; an early version of this file's own implementation accepted it by splitting userinfo at the first '@' wherever it fell

cases.name: dotted quad before the elision
cases.why: RFC 4291 §2.2: the dotted quad spells the address's LAST 32 bits, so it cannot precede the '::' elision

cases.name: userinfo with a bracketed host and a port
cases.why: §3.2: the control for the rows above — userinfo IS stripped when the authority does not open with a bracket, and the IPv6 host is then checked

cases.name: space in the authority
cases.why: §3.2.2: a reg-name is unreserved, pct-encoded or sub-delims

cases.name: absolute uri with query and fragment
cases.why: §3: the full production

cases.name: urn
cases.why: §3.3: path-rootless after the scheme

cases.name: ssh remote
cases.why: §3.2.1: userinfo is part of the authority

cases.name: uppercase scheme
cases.why: §3.1: a scheme is case-insensitive, so the uppercase spelling is the same URI

cases.name: scheme with an empty path
cases.why: §3: hier-part may be path-empty. ajv rejects this and is wrong

cases.name: host and port read as a scheme
cases.why: §3: 'host' is the scheme and '8080/p' a path-rootless. It validates for the wrong reason, which is why a host:port belongs in a uri-reference

cases.name: drive letter read as a scheme
cases.why: §3.1: a one-letter scheme is legal, so a Windows path validates by being misread — a separator swap alone does not make one a URI

cases.name: rooted path
cases.why: §4.3: a URI requires a scheme; only a uri-reference admits a relative path

cases.name: relative path
cases.why: §4.3: no scheme

cases.name: scheme starting with a digit
cases.why: §3.1: a scheme starts with ALPHA

cases.name: non-ascii host
cases.why: §2 is ASCII-only. santhosh-tekuri accepts this and is wrong

cases.name: non-ascii in the path
cases.why: §2 is ASCII-only, so the UTF-8 has to be percent-encoded

cases.name: empty string
cases.why: §3: a URI is at least a scheme and a colon
